title: Review: Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C8#c11 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C8#c05 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C8#c07 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C8#c09 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: C8#q10, C8#q13, C8#q17, C8#q19, C8#q08, C8#q15, C8#q18, C8#q23, C8#q07, C8#q14, C8#q16, C8#q22. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Igneous rock
items.clue: Rock formed when magma or lava cools and becomes solid.

items.label: Mantle
items.clue: The layer below the crust, about 2900 km thick: the thickest layer.

items.label: Inner core
items.clue: The centre of the Earth, made of solid metal, mainly iron and nickel.

items.label: Rock cycle
items.clue: The slow processes by which rocks form, are broken down and are turned into other types of rock.

questions.stem: Plant roots grow into cracks in a rock. As the roots grow, they split the rock apart. What is this?

options.text: Not a kind of weathering
Erosion of the rock
A metamorphic change
Biological weathering

questions.explanation: Yes. Living things can break rock up where it is. Roots widening cracks is biological weathering.

questions.stem: Coal and metal ores are called limited, or finite, resources. Why?

options.text: Only a few countries may mine them
They form far too slowly to be replaced
There is only a small amount of each
Using them destroys the atoms in them

questions.explanation: Yes. Coal and ores formed over millions of years, far too slowly to be replaced. So there is a fixed amount, and once it has been used it will run out.

questions.stem: Dry air contains nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), argon (Ar) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Which describes dry air?

options.text: A mixture of elements and a compound
A mixture of compounds and an element
Nitrogen and oxygen joined together
A pure substance when it is clean

questions.explanation: Yes. N₂, O₂ and Ar each contain one type of atom, so they are elements; CO₂ is a compound. They are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.

questions.stem: How do greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, keep the Earth warmer?

options.text: They let in more of the Sun's rays
They make a hole in the ozone layer
They absorb heat given off by the Earth
They burn in the air, giving out heat

questions.explanation: Yes. Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which then gives off heat (infrared). Greenhouse gases absorb some of this heat and send some back towards the Earth, keeping it warmer.

options.text: Rock melts deep underground, then cools again
Layers of sediment are pressed and cemented
Rain and wind slowly change the rock's surface
Heat and pressure change rock without melting it

questions.explanation: Yes. Deep underground, or near hot magma, heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it. For example, limestone becomes marble.

questions.stem: Which of these is a renewable resource?

options.text: Wood, because new trees can be planted
Aluminium, because cans can be recycled
Coal, because plants keep on growing
Iron ore, because there is so much of it

questions.explanation: Yes. A renewable resource can be replaced as fast as we use it. New trees can be grown to replace those cut down.

questions.stem: Which statement about dry air is correct?

options.text: Oxygen makes up about four-fifths of it
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths of it
Carbon dioxide makes up about a fifth of it
Its nitrogen and oxygen are chemically joined

questions.explanation: Yes. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, roughly four-fifths. Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth.

questions.stem: As the Earth's average temperature rises, which change do scientists expect?

options.text: Sea level rises as ice melts
Sea level falls as seas evaporate
Earthquakes become more common
Rivers fill up with more litter

questions.explanation: Yes. Ice on land melts and seawater expands as it warms, so sea level rises. It has already risen by about 20 cm since 1900.

options.text: Wet mud and sand just dry out and harden
Layers of sediment are squashed and cemented
Sediment melts near a volcano, then cools again
It rises up from deep inside the Earth

questions.explanation: Yes. Sediment settles in layers, and the weight of new layers squashes (compacts) it. Minerals from the water then cement the grains together.

questions.stem: Example figures for 1 kg of a metal: making it from ore uses 170 MJ (megajoules). Recycling scrap uses 4 MJ to collect it and 10 MJ to melt it. How much energy does recycling save?

options.text: 156 MJ
160 MJ
166 MJ
170 MJ

questions.explanation: Yes. Recycling uses 4 MJ + 10 MJ = 14 MJ. That is 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ less than making the metal from ore.

questions.stem: About what percentage of dry air is carbon dioxide?

options.text: About 0.04%
About 0.9%
About 4%
About 21%

questions.explanation: Yes. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of dry air, roughly 4 particles in every 10 000. Even so, it has an important effect on the Earth's temperature.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air. Can a rise in this small amount change the climate, and why?

options.text: No, as 0.04% is far too little to matter
Yes, as CO₂ absorbs heat from the Earth
Yes, as it is a poison that pollutes the air
No, as CO₂ does not absorb any heat at all

questions.explanation: Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs heat given off by the Earth, so even a small rise traps more heat. It has risen from about 0.028% before 1800 to about 0.042% in 2024, and the Earth has warmed.
